warnings: Neuropsychiatric symptoms (paediatric) — counsel observation.
monitoring: Clinical response; respiratory symptoms.

indications.text: Herpes zoster (shingles) — preferred over aciclovir for compliance

mechanism: Prodrug — hepatic + intestinal hydrolysis to aciclovir → viral thymidine kinase phosphorylation → inhibits viral DNA polymerase. ~ 3–5× higher oral bioavailability than aciclovir.

adult.regimen: Zoster: 1 g three times daily for 7 days (within 72 h of rash). HSV first episode: 500 mg twice daily for 10 days. Recurrent HSV: 500 mg twice daily for 3 days. Suppression: 500 mg once daily.

pregnancy.notes: Safe across pregnancy; first-line for HSV / VZV in pregnancy.

warnings: AKI risk in dehydration / elderly — maintain hydration.
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura reported in immunocompromised.
monitoring: Creatinine for prolonged courses.

mechanism: Inhibits bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase → blocks protein synthesis. Active against S. aureus (including MRSA), S. pyogenes.

adult.regimen: Cream apply thinly three times daily for 5 days. Nasal: apply 2 % ointment to each nostril twice daily for 5 days (MRSA decolonisation).

paediatric.frequency: Same regimen.

pregnancy.notes: Safe (minimal absorption).

warnings: Stewardship: emerging resistance with widespread use; limit to 5 days. Reserve for genuine MRSA decolonisation in clinical / outbreak settings.
monitoring: Re-evaluate at 5–10 days.

indications.text: MRSA skin / soft tissue infection (oral / IV)
MDR-TB / XDR-TB (component of BPaL / longer regimen)

mechanism: Binds 50S ribosomal subunit → prevents formation of 70S initiation complex. Bacteriostatic; bactericidal against streptococci.

adult.regimen: 600 mg twice daily (100 % oral bioavailability — same dose IV).
600 mg every 12 h.

paediatric.frequency: 10 mg/kg every 8 h (< 12 y) or every 12 h (≥ 12 y).

pregnancy.notes: Limited human data; reserve for MDR-TB / VRE where no alternative.

contraindications: Concurrent serotonergic agent without close monitoring (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs, triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, pethidine, methylene blue, St John's wort).
warnings: Linezolid is a REVERSIBLE MAOI — serotonin syndrome with serotonergics, hypertensive crisis with tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, beer, soy).
Myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia, anaemia) — risk increases > 14 days. Weekly FBC.
Peripheral + optic neuropathy with > 28-day use.
Lactic acidosis (rare).

adverseEffects.effect: Serotonin syndrome, lactic acidosis, severe myelosuppression

monitoring: FBC weekly. Visual + neurological symptoms reviewed; eye exam if > 28 days.

indications.text: Chloroquine-resistant uncomplicated malaria (oral, with doxycycline / clindamycin)

mechanism: Inhibits parasite haem polymerisation → free haem accumulates → parasite death.

adult.regimen: Loading: 20 mg/kg infused over 4 h (max 1.4 g). Then 10 mg/kg every 8 h over 4 h. Switch to oral when tolerated to complete 7 days.
Oral: 600 mg three times daily for 7 days + doxycycline 200 mg/day or clindamycin 7 days.

paediatric.frequency: Same weight-banded dosing as adults.

pregnancy.notes: Used in severe malaria in pregnancy when IV artesunate unavailable (artesunate preferred per WHO 2023).

warnings: Cinchonism — tinnitus, headache, nausea, blurred vision (dose-related).
QT prolongation + risk of torsades — concurrent QT drugs.
Hypoglycaemia — stimulates pancreatic insulin release; rebound common in pregnancy / severe malaria.
Haemolysis in G6PD-deficient.
monitoring: Continuous ECG during IV infusion. Glucose every 4 h. Daily parasitaemia.

indications.text: Radical cure of P. vivax / P. ovale (eliminates liver hypnozoites)
Single low-dose gametocytocide for P. falciparum transmission blocking (WHO 2012)

mechanism: Active metabolite (carboxyprimaquine) generates reactive oxygen species in plasmodial mitochondria — kills hypnozoites + gametocytes.

adult.regimen: P. vivax / ovale radical cure: 30 mg base once daily for 14 days (G6PD-normal). Falciparum transmission block: 0.25 mg/kg single dose.

paediatric.frequency: 0.5 mg/kg/day for 14 days (G6PD-normal).

pregnancy.notes: Avoid in pregnancy + breastfeeding (foetal G6PD status unknown). Use chloroquine prophylaxis 1×/week throughout pregnancy + radical cure post-partum if G6PD-normal.

warnings: G6PD testing MANDATORY before standard dosing — quantitative (not just qualitative) preferred in females (X-linked heterozygotes can be partial deficiency).
Single low dose (0.25 mg/kg) for P. falciparum transmission blocking is WHO-safe in mild G6PD deficiency.
Methaemoglobinaemia (CYP2D6 poor-metaboliser).
monitoring: G6PD status before dosing. Hb at day 7 of treatment if G6PD-intermediate.

indications.text: Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei — endemic in SE Asia)

mechanism: PBP-3 binding cell-wall inhibition; potent activity against Pseudomonas but weak Gram-positive cover.

adult.regimen: 1–2 g IV every 8 h (max 6 g/day). Melioidosis intensive phase: 50 mg/kg every 6 h × 2 weeks.

paediatric.frequency: 50 mg/kg every 8 h (max 6 g/day).

pregnancy.notes: Safe for serious infection.

warnings: Less Gram-positive cover than ceftriaxone — not for streptococcal / staphylococcal monotherapy.
Neurotoxicity (encephalopathy) in renal impairment.
monitoring: FBC, U&E, LFT.

mechanism: 30S ribosomal binding — same as gentamicin; broader Gram-negative cover including some gentamicin-resistant strains.

adult.regimen: 15 mg/kg ideal body weight once daily; target peak 25–35 mg/L, trough < 5 mg/L.

paediatric.frequency: 15 mg/kg once daily.

renal.adjustment: Same dose, extend interval to 36 h with TDM.

pregnancy.notes: Limited data — same fetal cranial nerve VIII risk as gentamicin.

warnings: Nephro + ototoxic — same precautions as gentamicin (TDM, avoid concurrent loop diuretic / vancomycin).
monitoring: Trough pre-dose; eGFR daily; audiology if > 7 days.

mechanism: B28 Pro → Asp substitution → does not self-associate as hexamer → rapid SC absorption (onset 10–20 min, peak 1–3 h, duration 3–5 h).

adult.regimen: Pre-meal: 0.05–0.15 U/kg per meal titrated to post-prandial glucose < 10 mmol/L. Inject 5–10 min before meal (or with the meal). Total daily insulin 0.5–1 U/kg in T1DM (50 % basal / 50 % bolus split).

paediatric.frequency: Same per-kg dose as adults; carbohydrate-counting ratios from ~ 1 U per 12 g in adolescents.

pregnancy.notes: Safer than regular insulin in pregnancy (less post-prandial hypoglycaemia).

warnings: Take immediately before meal — earlier than regular insulin.
Lipohypertrophy if injection sites not rotated.
monitoring: Capillary glucose 4–6× daily on multi-dose injection regimen.

indications.text: Newborn vitamin K deficiency bleeding prevention
Vitamin K deficiency in cholestatic liver disease / malabsorption

mechanism: Cofactor for hepatic γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X + proteins C and S.

adult.regimen: Warfarin reversal: 1–10 mg IV slow (over ≥ 30 sec). Major bleed: 10 mg IV + PCC 25–50 IU/kg. Asymptomatic INR 5–8: 1–2.5 mg oral. INR > 8: 1–5 mg oral.
Cholestatic liver disease: 10 mg orally weekly.

paediatric.frequency: Newborn prophylaxis: 1 mg IM single dose within 1 h of birth (UK + WHO). Oral alternative 2 mg at birth, day 4–7, and 1 month (less effective; reserved for parental refusal of IM).

pregnancy.notes: Safe; given to mother on warfarin / phenytoin in last 4 weeks to prevent neonatal haemorrhage.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity (anaphylactoid reaction to IV preparation rare).
warnings: Slow IV administration (anaphylactoid reactions reported with rapid push).
IV / IM preferred over subcutaneous (unreliable absorption).
Recheck INR at 6–12 h after vitamin K administration in warfarin reversal.
monitoring: INR 6–12 h after dose in warfarin reversal.

indications.text: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) — prevention + treatment

mechanism: Replaces deficient endogenous surfactant → reduces alveolar surface tension → prevents end-expiratory collapse, improves compliance + oxygenation.

adult.regimen: Neonatal use only. Loading 200 mg/kg intratracheal; repeat 100 mg/kg every 12 h up to 2 additional doses if persistent RDS.

pregnancy.notes: Not applicable (neonatal use).

contraindications: Pulmonary haemorrhage at time of administration (relative).
warnings: Transient airway obstruction during dosing — reflux up the tube; pause and resume.
Transient bradycardia / desaturation during administration.
Risk of pulmonary haemorrhage — particularly in PDA-shunting infants.
monitoring: Continuous SpO₂, ECG, respiratory rate during + after administration.

references.label: European Consensus Guidelines on Management of RDS (2023)

indications.text: Emergency contraception within 72 h of unprotected intercourse

mechanism: Primarily inhibits / delays ovulation. Less effective post-ovulation. Does NOT terminate established pregnancy.

adult.regimen: 1.5 mg single dose within 72 h of unprotected intercourse (sooner = more effective; 95 % efficacy < 24 h). Repeat dose if vomits within 3 h.

pregnancy.notes: Not abortifacient. Safe if accidentally taken after conception — no teratogenic signal.

warnings: Reduced efficacy if BMI > 26 (or weight > 70 kg) — consider doubling to 3 mg OR using ulipristal acetate (30 mg) OR copper IUD (most effective).
Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, ritonavir, St John's wort) reduce efficacy — use copper IUD as alternative.
If menses delayed > 7 days → urine pregnancy test.
monitoring: Pregnancy test if menses delayed > 7 days.

indications.text: Medical termination of pregnancy (with misoprostol) up to 70 days gestation
Medical management of missed / incomplete miscarriage
Cervical priming before surgical termination / induction of labour

mechanism: Competitive progesterone-receptor antagonist → decidual breakdown + cervical softening + increased uterine sensitivity to prostaglandins.

adult.regimen: MTOP ≤ 70 days: 200 mg orally, followed 24–48 h later by misoprostol 800 µg buccal / vaginal / sublingual. Missed miscarriage: 200 mg orally + misoprostol 800 µg 24–48 h later.

pregnancy.notes: Used DURING pregnancy for intentional termination only. AVOID if continuing pregnancy.

lactation: Brief interruption of breastfeeding (4 h) acceptable.
warnings: Rare severe bacterial sepsis (Clostridium sordellii) — counsel return for severe pain, weakness, prolonged bleeding.
Significant bleeding (10–20 % require additional intervention, 1–2 % surgical evacuation, 0.3 % transfusion).
Confirm completion at 7–14 days (urine pregnancy test or follow-up).

adverseEffects.effect: Vaginal bleeding (heavier than menses 5–14 days), abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea

monitoring: Confirm completion at 7–14 days. Beta-hCG decline / repeat scan if uncertain. Counsel about future contraception.

mechanism: Suppresses ovulation + thickens cervical mucus + thins endometrium.

adult.regimen: 150 mg IM every 12 weeks (Depo-Provera) OR 104 mg subcutaneous every 13 weeks (Sayana Press — self-administered).

pregnancy.notes: Not for use during pregnancy.

lactation: Compatible. Can be initiated immediately post-partum, including in breastfeeding women.
warnings: Bone-mineral-density loss (partly reversible) — consider use < 2 years where alternative available; not first-line in adolescents / women > 45.
Weight gain common (~ 2 kg / 1st year).
Return to fertility delayed up to 12 months after stopping (mean 5 months).
Counsel breakthrough bleeding.

adverseEffects.effect: Amenorrhoea, irregular bleeding, weight gain, mood disturbance
Reduced BMD, delayed return of fertility

monitoring: BP at each visit; review every 2 years for ongoing need (BMD).

mechanism: Oestrogen + progestogen → suppress hypothalamic GnRH → suppress LH surge → no ovulation.

adult.regimen: Take 1 tablet daily at same time for 21 days, then 7-day break (or continuous extended-cycle 84 + 7). Levonorgestrel 150 µg / ethinylestradiol 30 µg is first-line low-strength preparation.

pregnancy.notes: Not for use during pregnancy.

lactation: AVOID until ≥ 6 weeks post-partum + good lactation established (reduces milk supply). Progestogen-only preferred.
contraindications: History of VTE / arterial thrombosis / known thrombophilia.
warnings: VTE risk 3–5× background (highest in first year and after restart).
Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, ritonavir, St John's wort) reduce contraceptive efficacy → use alternative.
Missed pill rules — emergency contraception if > 1 pill missed in week 1.

adverseEffects.effect: Nausea, breast tenderness, breakthrough bleeding, mood change, headache

monitoring: BP at start + 3 months + annually.

references.label: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

indications.text: Iron-deficiency anaemia — intolerance / malabsorption / urgent / severe (Hb < 8 + symptomatic)
Heart failure with iron deficiency (CONFIRM-HF trial)

mechanism: Slow release of iron from carboxymaltose complex → bypasses GI absorption → restores iron stores within hours.

adult.regimen: Up to 1000 mg in a single infusion (maximum 20 mg/kg) given over ≥ 15 min. Repeat 1 week later if total replacement needs > 1000 mg.

pregnancy.notes: Safe from second trimester onwards. Particularly useful in third trimester for rapid correction before delivery.

warnings: Hypersensitivity / anaphylaxis (rare but reported) — observe 30 min post-infusion. Resuscitation equipment + adrenaline available.
Hypophosphataemia (often asymptomatic, may persist months) — check phosphate at 2 weeks + 3 months if repeated infusions.
Skin discoloration if extravasation.
monitoring: Hb + ferritin at 6–8 weeks. Phosphate at 2 weeks + 3 months if repeat doses.

references.label: ESC Heart Failure Guidelines (iron in HFrEF)

mechanism: Inhibits bacterial dihydropteroate synthase + has anti-neutrophil / anti-inflammatory effects in dermatologic indications.

adult.regimen: PJP prophylaxis: 100 mg once daily. Leprosy MB: 100 mg daily. Dermatitis herpetiformis: start 50 mg daily, titrate to effect (max 300 mg).

paediatric.frequency: 1 mg/kg/day (PJP / leprosy).

pregnancy.notes: Acceptable for leprosy / dermatitis herpetiformis; add folic acid 5 mg.

lactation: Acceptable; observe infant for haemolysis if G6PD-deficient.
warnings: G6PD screening before starting — methaemoglobinaemia + haemolysis.
Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis) — HLA-B*1301 risk in Asian populations.
Methaemoglobinaemia + sulfhaemoglobinaemia common — monitor SpO₂ vs PaO₂ gap.
Peripheral neuropathy with chronic use.

adverseEffects.effect: Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome, severe haemolysis (G6PD), agranulocytosis

monitoring: FBC + reticulocytes + methaemoglobin at 1 month then 6-monthly. LFT 3-monthly.

indications.text: Asthma maintenance — always in combination with ICS (never monotherapy)

mechanism: Selective β2-receptor agonist → bronchodilation (onset 10–20 min, duration 12 h).

adult.regimen: 50 µg twice daily (max 100 µg twice daily). Always in combination with ICS for asthma — never monotherapy (SMART trial — increased asthma deaths).

paediatric.frequency: Age ≥ 5: 50 µg twice daily, always with ICS.

pregnancy.notes: Limited data; ICS + LABA continued for asthma control.

contraindications: Asthma without concurrent ICS (FDA / EMA boxed warning).
warnings: ASTHMA: NEVER as monotherapy — increases mortality. Always combination ICS+LABA inhaler.
β-blocker (propranolol — non-selective) antagonises bronchodilation.
QT prolongation at high doses, tremor, palpitations.
monitoring: Symptom control, inhaler technique, FEV1.

indications.text: COPD maintenance — reduces exacerbations + improves FEV1
Severe asthma (add-on to ICS + LABA, ≥ 6 years)

mechanism: Selective M3 muscarinic-receptor antagonist → bronchodilation. Long duration (24 h).

adult.regimen: 18 µg via HandiHaler OR 5 µg via Respimat once daily, same time each day.

pregnancy.notes: Limited data; only if benefit > risk.

warnings: Acute angle-closure glaucoma — counsel ocular pain, halos.
Urinary retention in BPH.
AVOID concurrent inhaled ipratropium (additive anticholinergic).
monitoring: FEV1, exacerbation frequency, intra-ocular symptoms.

indications.text: Paediatric / neonatal hypoglycaemia (preferred over 50 % in children — avoids sclerosis)

mechanism: Cellular substrate — restores plasma glucose; less sclerotic than 50 % in small veins.

adult.regimen: Adult hypoglycaemia: 100 mL of 10 % IV bolus over 5 min (10 g glucose); alternative to 50 % when small vein. Sulphonylurea maintenance: 5–10 % infusion at maintenance + 50 % above with octreotide.

paediatric.frequency: Hypoglycaemia: 2 mL/kg of 10 % IV bolus, recheck at 5 + 15 min. Neonatal maintenance: 60–80 mL/kg/day of 10 % dextrose in the first 24 h.

pregnancy.notes: Safe.

warnings: Rebound hypoglycaemia after bolus alone — follow with 10 % infusion + recheck.
Hyperglycaemic stress in critical illness — target glucose 7–10 mmol/L.
monitoring: Glucose every 15 min post-bolus + hourly during infusion.

indications.text: Opioid use disorder — opioid agonist therapy (OAT)

mechanism: Full µ-opioid agonist; long half-life (24–55 h). Cross-tolerant with heroin / morphine — blocks withdrawal + reduces craving + occupies receptors so additional opioid has no effect.

adult.regimen: OAT initiation: 10–30 mg orally on day 1 (titrate based on objective opioid withdrawal scale + tolerance). Titrate by 5–10 mg every 3–5 days to effective dose (typically 60–120 mg/day). Daily-supervised dispensing first 3 months.

pregnancy.notes: Maintain or initiate methadone in pregnancy (avoiding withdrawal prevents miscarriage / preterm labour). Dose may need increase in third trimester (split BID). Neonatal abstinence syndrome managed in neonatal unit.

warnings: QT prolongation — torsades de pointes risk especially > 100 mg/day; baseline + 30 days + annual ECG. Avoid with QT drugs (azithromycin, fluconazole, ondansetron, haloperidol, amiodarone, clarithromycin).
Respiratory depression — high risk in early induction (long half-life accumulates over 5–7 days).
Severe drug interactions — CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) → withdrawal; inhibitors → toxicity.
Overdose — naloxone repeated / infusion due to long methadone half-life.

adverseEffects.effect: Torsades de pointes, respiratory depression, overdose death

monitoring: ECG at baseline, 30 days, annually + dose > 100 mg. Urine drug screen periodic. Pregnancy test where applicable.

references.label: NICE TA114 — Methadone + buprenorphine for opioid dependence

indications.text: Opioid use disorder — OAT (alternative to methadone, often preferred for safety)

mechanism: High-affinity partial µ-agonist with ceiling effect on respiratory depression (safer than full agonist in overdose). Displaces other opioids — can precipitate withdrawal if started too soon after heroin / methadone.

adult.regimen: Induction (must be in mild objective withdrawal, COWS ≥ 7): 4 mg sublingually, second 4 mg dose 2–4 h later (total 8 mg day 1). Titrate to 8–16 mg/day; max 32 mg. Suboxone (with naloxone) preferred to deter injection misuse.

pregnancy.notes: Buprenorphine acceptable; less neonatal abstinence severity than methadone (MOTHER trial). Use mono-buprenorphine (Subutex) — Suboxone naloxone has limited safety data.

warnings: Precipitated withdrawal — start ONLY when in objective opioid withdrawal (12–24 h after last short-acting opioid; 36–48 h after methadone).
Hepatic injury — LFTs at baseline + periodic.
Sublingual administration — DO NOT swallow; takes 5–10 min to dissolve.
monitoring: LFT baseline + 6-monthly. Urine drug screen periodic.

indications.text: Opioid use disorder — relapse prevention (after detoxification)
Alcohol use disorder — reduces heavy-drinking days, craving

mechanism: Pure opioid antagonist — blocks reinforcing effects of opioids. In alcohol disorder, blocks endogenous opioid reward.

adult.regimen: Alcohol / opioid: 50 mg orally once daily. Start AFTER at least 7 days opioid-free (10 days methadone) — naloxone challenge to confirm.
Vivitrol depot: 380 mg IM monthly.

pregnancy.notes: Limited data; only if benefit > risk.

contraindications: Current opioid use / dependence (precipitates severe withdrawal).
warnings: Precipitates SEVERE withdrawal if started < 7 days opioid-free.
Patients who relapse have lost tolerance — increased overdose death risk.
Counsel: in emergency needing opioid analgesia, use 2–3× normal dose carefully or non-opioid alternative.
Hepatotoxicity at high doses.

adverseEffects.effect: Severe opioid withdrawal (in dependent users), hepatotoxicity (high dose)

monitoring: LFT baseline + 3-monthly.

references.label: NICE TA115 — Naltrexone for opioid dependence

indications.text: Severe pain (acute trauma, war / disaster setting)

mechanism: NMDA receptor antagonism + opioid-mu agonism + monoamine reuptake inhibition. Preserves airway reflexes + spontaneous breathing.

adult.regimen: Procedural sedation: 1–2 mg/kg IV over 1 min, supplement 0.5 mg/kg as needed. Analgesia (sub-dissociative): 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV / IM. Induction for intubation: 1–2 mg/kg IV.
Procedural sedation: 4–5 mg/kg IM.

paediatric.frequency: Sedation: 1 mg/kg IV (or 4–5 mg/kg IM).

pregnancy.notes: Reserve for serious indication; theoretical neurodevelopmental concerns from prolonged exposure.

contraindications: Raised intracranial pressure (debated — recent evidence weak).
warnings: Emergence phenomena (hallucinations, vivid dreams) — pre-medicate with low-dose midazolam in adults if elective sedation.
Hypersalivation — atropine / glycopyrrolate pre-medication.
Counsel risk of street ketamine misuse (urinary tract toxicity).

adverseEffects.effect: Emergence phenomena, hypersalivation, nystagmus, hypertension, tachycardia

monitoring: Continuous SpO₂, ECG, BP during dissociative sedation.

mechanism: GABA-A receptor positive modulator → CNS depression. Rapid onset (30 sec), brief duration.

adult.regimen: Induction: 1.5–2.5 mg/kg slow IV (lower in elderly / shock). ICU sedation: 0.3–4 mg/kg/h titrated. AVOID > 4 mg/kg/h for > 48 h (PRIS risk).

paediatric.frequency: Induction 2.5–3.5 mg/kg ≥ 3 y. ICU sedation > 16 y only.

pregnancy.notes: Used in obstetric anaesthesia; neonatal depression if delivered close to induction.

contraindications: ICU sedation in paediatric patients < 16 y (PRIS).
warnings: Hypotension on induction — fluid bolus + reduce dose in shock.
Apnoea — be ready to ventilate.
Propofol-related infusion syndrome (PRIS) — high-dose long-duration; metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, hyperkalaemia. Limit dose > 4 mg/kg/h to < 48 h.
Counsel: green discolouration of urine harmless.
monitoring: Continuous BP, SpO₂, ECG. CK + lactate + ABG if prolonged high-dose infusion.

indications.text: Fever where oral route not available

mechanism: Same as oral — central COX inhibition.

adult.regimen: 1 g IV infusion over 15 min every 6 h (max 4 g/24 h). Reduce to 500 mg if < 50 kg.

paediatric.frequency: 15 mg/kg every 6 h (max 4 doses/24 h).

pregnancy.notes: Safe — same as oral.

warnings: Dose errors more common with IV (mg vs mL confusion) — double-check.
Underweight adults < 50 kg → max 60 mg/kg/day.
Hepatotoxicity same as oral in overdose.
monitoring: LFT for prolonged courses, or in malnutrition / alcohol / hepatic disease.

indications.text: COPD with frequent exacerbations / eosinophilic phenotype

mechanism: Local glucocorticoid receptor activation → anti-inflammatory airway effect. Strong topical potency, low oral bioavailability (high first-pass), reduced systemic effects.

adult.regimen: Asthma: low dose 200–400 µg/day; medium 400–800 µg/day; high 800–1600 µg/day in 1–2 divided doses.
Croup: 2 mg nebulised single dose (children). Acute asthma adjunct in some protocols.

paediatric.frequency: Children 5–11 y low 100–200 µg/day, medium 200–400, high > 400 — always via spacer.

pregnancy.notes: Safe — preferred ICS in pregnancy; most safety data of any ICS.

warnings: Inhaler-technique check every visit; use spacer for pMDI.
Rinse mouth after each dose (oral candidiasis, dysphonia).
High-dose long-term: HPA-axis suppression, growth velocity reduction in children, cataracts.
monitoring: Asthma control, growth velocity in children, inhaler technique.

indications.text: Ulcerative colitis — induction + maintenance of remission
Crohn's colitis (less effective than for UC)

mechanism: Inhibits NF-κB + lipoxygenase + cyclo-oxygenase pathways in colonic mucosa; topical effect.

adult.regimen: UC induction: 2.4–4.8 g/day in divided doses. Maintenance: 1.5–2.4 g/day. Modified-release formulations target ileum / colon.
Distal UC: enema 1 g at bedtime OR suppository 500 mg three times daily for 4–6 weeks.

pregnancy.notes: Safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding — first-line UC maintenance.

warnings: Renal toxicity (interstitial nephritis) — check eGFR baseline + annually.
Blood dyscrasias (rare) — counsel sore throat, fever, bleeding.
Pancreatitis (rare).

adverseEffects.effect: Nausea, headache, abdominal pain, diarrhoea (paradoxically can worsen colitis)
Interstitial nephritis, hepatitis, pancreatitis, blood dyscrasias

monitoring: FBC + U&E + LFT baseline, at 3 months, then annually.

mechanism: Same as simvastatin — minimal CYP3A4 (mainly CYP2C9 + OATP1B1) → fewer DDIs.

adult.regimen: 5–40 mg once daily. Start 10 mg, titrate by LDL response. Reduce in Asian descent (genetic OATP1B1 — higher exposure).

pregnancy.notes: Avoid in pregnancy + breastfeeding.

warnings: Less affected by CYP3A4 inhibitors than simvastatin / atorvastatin.
Proteinuria + microscopic haematuria at high doses (40 mg).
Asian populations — higher AUC; start lower.
monitoring: LFT baseline + 3 + 12 months.

mechanism: Direct competitive inhibitor of free + clot-bound thrombin (factor IIa).

adult.regimen: AF: 150 mg twice daily (110 mg if age ≥ 80, increased bleed risk, or concurrent verapamil). DVT/PE: 5–10 days of parenteral anticoagulation then 150 mg twice daily.

pregnancy.notes: Avoid; use LMWH in pregnancy.

warnings: P-gp inhibitors (verapamil, amiodarone, clarithromycin, dronedarone, ketoconazole) raise levels.
Reversal: idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5 g IV — specific antidote.
Dyspepsia common — take with full glass of water.
monitoring: eGFR + Hb 6-monthly.

mechanism: Selective direct factor Xa inhibition.

adult.regimen: 60 mg once daily. Reduce to 30 mg if any of: CrCl 15–50, weight ≤ 60 kg, concurrent strong P-gp inhibitor (verapamil, dronedarone, clarithromycin, ketoconazole).

pregnancy.notes: Avoid; use LMWH.

contraindications: eGFR > 95 in AF (reduced efficacy vs warfarin).
warnings: P-gp inhibitor / inducer interaction.
DVT/PE needs 5–10 days parenteral first.
monitoring: eGFR + Hb 6-monthly.

mechanism: Inhibits Na-Cl co-transporter in distal tubule + vasodilation.

adult.regimen: 1.5 mg modified-release once daily (or 2.5 mg standard).

pregnancy.notes: Avoid first-line (volume depletion, electrolyte shift).

warnings: Hyponatraemia in elderly — check Na at 1 + 4 weeks of initiation.
Hyperuricaemia + gout flare.
QT prolongation at high doses.
monitoring: U&E + Na at 1 + 4 weeks then 6-monthly.

indications.text: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage — prevention of cerebral vasospasm + ischaemic neurological deficit

mechanism: L-type Ca channel blockade with preferential cerebrovascular effect.

adult.regimen: 60 mg every 4 h orally for 21 days starting within 96 h of SAH. NG if unable to swallow.

pregnancy.notes: Limited data; SAH is critical — use.

warnings: Hypotension common — adjust other antihypertensives.
Do NOT give IV (cardiac arrest reports).
monitoring: BP every 4 h during therapy.

indications.text: Raised intracranial pressure (TBI, stroke, hepatic encephalopathy)

mechanism: Inert osmotic agent — pulls fluid from intracellular / interstitial space → cerebral oedema reduction.

adult.regimen: Raised ICP: 0.5–1 g/kg of 20 % over 15 min, repeat every 4–6 h targeting osmolality 300–320 mOsm/L. Glaucoma: 1–2 g/kg over 30 min.

paediatric.frequency: 0.5–1 g/kg over 15 min, repeat every 4–6 h.

pregnancy.notes: Use only if benefit > risk; limited data.

warnings: Rebound ICP rise after stopping — taper.
Hyperosmolality, hypovolaemia, hypernatraemia + AKI risk.
Check osmolality + electrolytes every 6 h.
monitoring: Serum osmolality 6-hourly (target 300–320); Na, K, creatinine; urine output.

mechanism: Long-acting somatostatin analogue — inhibits GH, glucagon, insulin, splanchnic blood flow.

adult.regimen: Variceal bleed: 50 µg IV bolus + 50 µg/h infusion × 3–5 days.
Sulphonylurea overdose: 50–100 µg SC every 6 h × 24 h. Carcinoid: 50–250 µg SC three times daily.

pregnancy.notes: Limited data; reserve for serious indication.

warnings: Hyperglycaemia (suppresses insulin) — monitor glucose.
Gallstones (long-term use).
Bradycardia.
monitoring: Glucose during infusion. Thyroid + gallbladder USS for long-term.

indications.text: Acute oesophageal variceal bleeding (preferred over octreotide where available)

mechanism: V1-receptor agonist → splanchnic vasoconstriction → ↓ portal pressure.

pregnancy.notes: Manufacturer advises avoid unless essential — limited human data. (BNF)

warnings: Significant anticholinergic load — caution in elderly, frail, dementia (consider mirabegron alternative).
Hyperthermia in hot weather (reduced sweating).
Reduce dose in hepatic impairment.
adverseEffects: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, dizziness
Cognitive impairment, confusion (especially in elderly)
Urinary retention, tachycardia
monitoring: Cognitive function in elderly; bowel function

indications.text: Combined hormonal contraception; menstrual disorders in HRT formulations.

mechanism: Selective oestrogen-receptor agonist in target tissues (combined hormonal contraception, menstrual regulation).

adult.regimen: 20–35 micrograms daily as part of a combined formulation; 21/7 or extended regimens.

pregnancy: Contraindicated.
lactation: Avoid — combined oral contraceptives containing ethinylestradiol can suppress milk supply, especially in the first 6 weeks postpartum. Progestogen-only methods are preferred. (BNF; ABM Clinical Protocol #13; LactMed)
contraindications: Personal or strong family history of VTE
warnings: VTE risk highest in first 3 months of starting combined hormonal contraception.
Interacts with enzyme-inducing antiepileptics, rifampicin, St John's wort — additional contraception required.
adverseEffects: Breast tenderness, nausea
Spotting / breakthrough bleeding
Mood change, headache
Hypertension, VTE (rare but serious)
monitoring: BP at initiation and at least annually

indications.text: Adjunctive therapy in type 2 diabetes mellitus.

mechanism: Selective dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 inhibition → prolonged incretin (GLP-1) activity.

adult.regimen: 5 mg once daily (2.5 mg in moderate-severe renal impairment).

pregnancy.notes: Insufficient human data; insulin is the preferred agent for diabetes in pregnancy — switch before conception or at first confirmation of pregnancy. (BNF; NICE NG3)

lactation: No data on transfer into human milk; manufacturer advises avoid. Insulin or metformin preferred where pharmacotherapy is needed. (BNF)
warnings: Caution in heart failure (modest increase in hospitalisation in SAVOR-TIMI 53).
Reduce dose to 2.5 mg in moderate-severe renal impairment.
adverseEffects: Hypersensitivity reactions including angioedema
Acute pancreatitis (rare)
Mild GI upset
Increased HF hospitalisation in at-risk patients
monitoring: HbA1c every 3 months; renal function periodically

indications.text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus where other oral agents are inappropriate (withdrawn in EU/UK; included for cross-reference completeness).

mechanism: PPAR-γ agonism → improved insulin sensitivity in adipose, hepatic and skeletal muscle.

adult.regimen: No longer recommended; 4–8 mg/day historic.

pregnancy.notes: Manufacturer contraindicates in pregnancy; withdrawn from many markets for cardiovascular safety. Switch to insulin. (BNF; EMA suspension 2010)

lactation: Excreted in animal milk; manufacturer advises avoid. (BNF)
warnings: Withdrawn from EU/UK; record retained for cross-reference and PGx review (CYP2C8).
adverseEffects: Weight gain, fluid retention, heart failure, fracture risk in women, hepatotoxicity
monitoring: LFTs at baseline and periodically; cardiac status

indications.text: Herpes simplex, varicella zoster, herpes-zoster ophthalmicus.

mechanism: Selective phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase to monophosphate, then cellular kinases to triphosphate → herpes-virus DNA polymerase chain-termination.

adult.regimen: 800 mg five times daily for 7 days, started within 72 h of rash.
10 mg/kg every 8 h for 14–21 days (adjust by CrCl).

pregnancy: Treatment of severe herpes simplex / VZV in pregnancy is appropriate; benefit outweighs risk.
warnings: Reduce dose in renal impairment — risk of crystalline nephropathy and neurotoxicity.
Maintain adequate hydration with IV therapy.
adverseEffects: GI upset
Rash
Crystalline nephropathy and AKI (especially rapid IV bolus)
Neurotoxicity (confusion, hallucination) at high serum levels
monitoring: Renal function before and during IV therapy
Neurology in elderly or renally impaired patients

indications.text: Solid-organ transplant immunosuppression, severe psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, refractory nephrotic syndrome.

mechanism: Cyclophilin-binding → calcineurin inhibition → reduced T-cell IL-2 transcription.

adult.regimen: Initial 10–15 mg/kg/day in two divided doses, taper guided by trough levels.
2.5–5 mg/kg/day in two divided doses; maximum 5 mg/kg/day; review at 8 weeks.

pregnancy: Use only if benefit outweighs risk; associated with prematurity and low birthweight.
lactation: Variable but generally low milk levels; recent guidance considers breastfeeding acceptable in stable transplant recipients with monitoring of infant ciclosporin levels and renal function. (LactMed)
contraindications: Severe renal impairment for non-transplant indications
warnings: Major CYP3A4 substrate and P-gp inhibitor — many interactions including statins (myopathy), grapefruit juice and azoles.
Nephrotoxicity is dose- and time-dependent; gum hyperplasia and hirsutism common.
Avoid live vaccines while immunosuppressed.
Renal cell and skin malignancy risk on long-term therapy.
adverseEffects: Renal impairment, hypertension
Tremor, paraesthesia, headache
Hirsutism, gingival hyperplasia
Hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia
Hyperlipidaemia
monitoring: Trough whole-blood ciclosporin level per indication
BP, U&E, LFTs, lipids, magnesium and uric acid

mechanism: Paramagnetic ion shortens T1 relaxation time → enhanced MRI signal.

adult.regimen: 0.1–0.2 mmol/kg IV per specific agent and indication.

pregnancy.notes: Avoid in pregnancy unless the diagnostic information is essential and cannot be obtained by non-contrast MRI — gadolinium crosses the placenta and has been associated with rare fetal effects. (ACR Manual on Contrast Media; RCR/RCOG guidance)

lactation: Less than 0.04% of an administered dose is excreted in milk and oral bioavailability in the infant is <1%; breastfeeding need not be interrupted after a standard dose. (LactMed; ACR Manual on Contrast Media)
contraindications: Severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30) — risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis with linear agents
warnings: Use macrocyclic agents in patients with renal impairment; check renal function before administration.
adverseEffects: Headache, nausea, injection-site reaction, anaphylactoid reaction (rare), NSF in severe renal impairment
monitoring: eGFR before administration in at-risk patients

indications.text: Iron-deficiency anaemia where oral iron is ineffective or not tolerated.

mechanism: Parenteral elemental iron donor replenishing transferrin-bound iron stores.

adult.regimen: 100–200 mg IV every 1–3 days up to calculated total iron deficit.

pregnancy.notes: Avoid in the first trimester; routinely used in the second and third trimesters for iron-deficiency anaemia unresponsive to or intolerant of oral iron. (BNF; NICE QS22)

lactation: Negligible transfer to milk and poor oral bioavailability in the infant; compatible with breastfeeding. (LactMed)
contraindications: Anaemia not due to iron deficiency
warnings: Anaphylactoid reactions — resuscitation equipment must be available; test dose may be required.
adverseEffects: Hypotension, nausea, taste disturbance, injection-site reactions, anaphylactoid reactions
monitoring: Hb, ferritin, transferrin saturation; observe 30 min after infusion

indications.text: Diagnostic radiographic procedures requiring iodinated contrast.

mechanism: Iodinated contrast media providing X-ray attenuation for CT and angiography.

adult.regimen: Per indication; typical volume 50–150 mL of 300–350 mg iodine/mL.

pregnancy.notes: Iodinated low-osmolar contrast crosses the placenta; use only when essential. No documented teratogenicity at diagnostic doses. (ACR Manual on Contrast Media)

lactation: Less than 1% of the maternal dose appears in milk and oral bioavailability in the infant is <1%; breastfeeding may continue uninterrupted. Neonatal thyroid screening should still be performed per routine. (LactMed; ACR Manual on Contrast Media)
contraindications: Severe iodine hypersensitivity (history of anaphylactoid reaction)
warnings: Risk of contrast-induced AKI in renal impairment, diabetes, dehydration — hydrate before and after.
adverseEffects: Warm sensation, nausea, anaphylactoid reactions, contrast-induced AKI, delayed skin reactions
monitoring: eGFR before and 48 h after administration in at-risk patients

mechanism: Topical nucleoside analogue inhibiting herpes-virus DNA polymerase at the site of application.

adult.regimen: Apply five times daily for 5–10 days.

pregnancy.notes: Minimal systemic absorption from topical application; considered compatible in pregnancy. (BNF; Briggs et al., 11th ed.)

lactation: Topical use is compatible with breastfeeding. (LactMed)
warnings: For external use only; apply within 1 h of prodrome for best effect.
adverseEffects: Local burning, stinging, mild erythema
monitoring: None

indications.text: Severe falciparum malaria (IV first-line per WHO).

mechanism: Endoperoxide bridge generates reactive radicals damaging Plasmodium proteins.

adult.regimen: 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h, then once daily for ≥ 24 h or until oral therapy possible (minimum 3 IV/IM doses).

pregnancy: Use in any trimester for severe malaria when benefit outweighs risk; preferred over quinine in severe disease.
lactation: Excreted in milk in small amounts; WHO recommends artesunate-based combinations in breastfeeding mothers where indicated for uncomplicated and severe malaria. (WHO Malaria Guidelines 2023; LactMed)
warnings: Delayed haemolysis 1–4 weeks after treatment in returning travellers — monitor Hb at 2, 3 and 4 weeks.
Always follow with full course of an effective oral antimalarial (e.g. artemether-lumefantrine).
Reconstitute IV solution immediately before use.
adverseEffects: Delayed haemolytic anaemia
Transient AST/ALT elevation
Headache, dizziness
Bradycardia (rare)
Hypersensitivity reactions
monitoring: Parasitaemia, Hb, parasite clearance during admission
Hb weekly for 4 weeks after discharge (delayed haemolysis)

indications.text: Threatened preterm labour 24–33 weeks (per local protocol).

mechanism: Competitive oxytocin- and vasopressin-receptor antagonism on uterine smooth muscle.

adult.regimen: Bolus 6.75 mg, then infusion 18 mg/h for 3 h, then 6 mg/h for up to 45 h (max 330 mg total).

pregnancy.notes: Licensed tocolytic used in pregnancy specifically to suppress preterm labour between 24 and 33+6 weeks. (BNF; NICE NG25)

lactation: Brief intrapartum exposure only; small amounts may be excreted in colostrum but considered compatible with breastfeeding once therapy is complete. (LactMed)
warnings: Limit to 48 hours; longer use not supported.
adverseEffects: Nausea, headache, hyperglycaemia, tachycardia, injection-site reaction
monitoring: Maternal HR, BP, fetal CTG

indications.text: Maintenance therapy in asthma and (combined) COPD.

mechanism: Glucocorticoid receptor agonist reducing airway inflammation; minimal systemic absorption from inhalation.

adult.regimen: 200–400 micrograms twice daily (low-dose ICS); 800–1000 micrograms twice daily (high dose).

pregnancy.notes: Inhaled corticosteroids are preferred to systemic steroids in pregnancy for asthma control; systemic absorption from inhalation is minimal and benefits of well-controlled asthma outweigh risks. (BNF; GINA 2024)

lactation: Inhaled corticosteroids produce negligible milk levels and are compatible with breastfeeding. (LactMed; BNF)
warnings: Oral candidiasis and dysphonia — rinse mouth after use and use spacer device.
Long-term high-dose use can suppress adrenal function in adults and impair growth in children.
adverseEffects: Oral candidiasis, hoarseness, sore throat, paradoxical bronchospasm (rare)
monitoring: Inhaler technique annually; growth in children

indications.text: Antenatal lung maturation 24–34 weeks; severe inflammatory disease.

mechanism: Long-acting glucocorticoid; antenatal administration accelerates fetal lung maturation.

adult.regimen: 12 mg IM, second dose at 24 h.
0.5–9 mg/day in divided doses depending on indication.

pregnancy.notes: Antenatal corticosteroid of choice for accelerating fetal lung maturation in threatened preterm birth between 24+0 and 34+6 weeks; benefits well established. (RCOG Green-top 7; NICE NG25)

lactation: Short courses produce low milk levels relative to physiological cortisol; compatible with breastfeeding. (LactMed)
warnings: Long-acting steroid — prolonged use carries high risk of HPA-axis suppression.
Antenatal use requires obstetric supervision and consideration of repeat course risks.
adverseEffects: Hyperglycaemia, weight gain, mood change, immunosuppression, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression
monitoring: BP, glucose, weight on prolonged use; bone density

indications.text: Lower UTI, skin and soft-tissue infection.

mechanism: Beta-lactam binding penicillin-binding proteins; bactericidal against Gram-positive cocci and some Gram-negatives.

adult.regimen: 500 mg every 8–12 h; up to 1 g every 6 h in severe infection.

pregnancy.notes: Cephalosporins are considered safe across all trimesters; cefalexin is widely used for UTI in pregnancy. (BNF; Briggs et al., 11th ed.)

lactation: Small amounts in milk; compatible with breastfeeding. Monitor the infant for diarrhoea, candidiasis, or rash. (LactMed; BNF)
warnings: Caution if penicillin hypersensitivity (5–10% cross-reactivity).
Reduce dose in renal impairment.
adverseEffects: Diarrhoea, nausea
Rash, urticaria
Eosinophilia
C. difficile colitis (rare)
monitoring: None routinely required

indications.text: Chloroquine-sensitive malaria prophylaxis/treatment; rheumatological disease (where hydroxychloroquine unavailable).

mechanism: Concentrates in Plasmodium food vacuole inhibiting haem polymerisation; immunomodulatory in autoimmune disease.

adult.regimen: 310 mg base weekly, started 1 week before and continued 4 weeks after travel.
620 mg base at 0 and 6–8 h, then 310 mg daily for 2 days (total 1.55 g base).

pregnancy: Considered safe at prophylactic and treatment doses.
lactation: Excreted in milk in small amounts (relative infant dose 0.6–1%); compatible with breastfeeding for both malaria treatment/prophylaxis and rheumatological indications. (LactMed; WHO)
warnings: Cumulative dose > 100 g (typically > 5 years) increases retinopathy risk — baseline + annual ophthalmology screening.
Lowers seizure threshold; caution in epilepsy.
Hypoglycaemia risk — caution in diabetes on insulin/sulfonylureas.
adverseEffects: GI upset, headache, pruritus (especially in darker-skinned individuals)
Retinopathy (irreversible if late)
QT prolongation
Haemolysis in severe G6PD deficiency
monitoring: Baseline ophthalmology and 5-yearly during chronic use; ECG before initiation when QT-prolonging drugs co-prescribed

mechanism: Inhibits fungal 14-α-demethylase, reducing ergosterol synthesis.

adult.regimen: 500 mg pessary at night, single dose; or 200 mg pessary nightly × 3.
Apply 1% cream 2–3 times daily for 2–4 weeks.

pregnancy: Topical / vaginal use considered safe.
lactation: Topical and intravaginal use produce negligible systemic exposure; compatible with breastfeeding. Wipe nipple before feeding if applied there. (LactMed; BNF)
warnings: Pessaries may damage latex condoms and diaphragms — counsel patient.
adverseEffects: Local burning, irritation, mild skin reaction
monitoring: None routinely

mechanism: Selective oestrogen-receptor agonist restoring oestrogenic effects on menopausal target tissues.

pregnancy.notes: HRT is not indicated in pregnancy; manufacturer contraindicates. (BNF)

monitoring: BP, weight, breast and pelvic examination at annual review

indications.text: Maintenance therapy in asthma and COPD; intranasal in allergic rhinitis.

pregnancy.notes: Inhaled corticosteroids are preferred to systemic steroids in pregnancy for asthma control; minimal systemic absorption. (BNF; GINA 2024)

200 IU at birth, plus monovalent HB vaccine.

monitoring: HBsAg and anti-HBs follow-up per indication

contraindications: Pregnancy and pregnancy planning (highly teratogenic — washout required)
Severe immunodeficiency or active serious infection

Hepatotoxicity — discontinue if ALT > 3× ULN.
Pulmonary fibrosis / interstitial lung disease reported.

Alopecia
Hepatic enzyme elevation, hepatitis
Hypertension
Leucopenia

indications.text: Partial and secondarily generalised tonic-clonic seizures.

Rash including SJS/TEN; HLA-B*1502 carriers higher risk.

CYP3A4 substrate and inhibitor — many interactions.

adverseEffects: Flu-like symptoms, depression, leucopenia, thyroid dysfunction, autoimmune disease
monitoring: FBC, LFTs, TSH; mental state

indications.text: Atypical depression unresponsive to other antidepressants (per specialist).

mechanism: Irreversible inhibition of MAO-A and MAO-B → elevated synaptic monoamines; high tyramine-interaction risk.

adult.indication: Atypical depression unresponsive to other therapy
adult.regimen: 15 mg three times daily; max 90 mg/day; review at 4 weeks.

pregnancy.notes: Limited human data; MAOIs carry hypertensive-crisis risk and complicate obstetric anaesthesia and tocolysis. Avoid where alternatives exist. (BNF; Briggs et al., 11th ed.)

lactation: No human data; manufacturer advises avoid. (BNF; LactMed)
warnings: Tyramine-containing food reaction — counsel on dietary restrictions; specialist initiation only.
adverseEffects: Hypertensive crisis with tyramine/sympathomimetics, postural hypotension, weight gain, hepatotoxicity
monitoring: BP each visit; LFTs

indications.text: Prevention of invasive pneumococcal disease in adults (≥65 or high risk) and routine paediatric schedule.

mechanism: Antigenic polysaccharide (PPV23) or conjugate (PCV13/15/20) inducing serotype-specific antibody.

adult.regimen: 13- or 20-valent conjugate vaccine single dose; consider PPV23 booster per local schedule.

pregnancy.notes: Inactivated polysaccharide and conjugate pneumococcal vaccines may be given in pregnancy when indicated (e.g. asplenia, chronic disease). (WHO position paper; CDC ACIP; UK Green Book)

lactation: Inactivated vaccines are compatible with breastfeeding. (CDC ACIP; UK Green Book)
contraindications: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component
warnings: Live vaccines: avoid in immunosuppression and pregnancy. Counsel about expected mild fever/local reactions.
adverseEffects: Injection-site soreness, redness; low-grade fever; rare anaphylaxis
monitoring: 15-min observation post-injection where anaphylaxis kit not immediately available

references.label: WHO position paper on pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (2019)

indications.text: Severe nausea and vertigo, especially vestibular; previously used in psychosis.

mechanism: D2 receptor antagonism (chemoreceptor trigger zone) with sedative and antimuscarinic effects.

adult.regimen: 5–10 mg up to three times daily.
12.5 mg IM (deep).

pregnancy.notes: Used as a second-line antiemetic in pregnancy after first-line agents fail; no consistent teratogenic signal at therapeutic doses. (BNF; RCOG Green-top 69)

lactation: Limited data; small amounts in milk and case reports of infant sedation. Use occasionally and monitor the infant. (LactMed; BNF)
warnings: Extrapyramidal effects, especially in young women; QT prolongation; anticholinergic load.
adverseEffects: Dystonia, akathisia, drowsiness, hypotension, photosensitivity
monitoring: Watch for acute dystonia, particularly in first 48 h

indications.text: Luteal-phase support, prevention of preterm birth in selected women, HRT (with oestrogen).

mechanism: Selective progesterone-receptor agonist supporting luteal phase and pregnancy.

adult.regimen: 200–400 mg/day in 2 divided doses (micronised pessary).
200 mg nightly from second trimester per local protocol.

pregnancy.notes: Vaginal progesterone is recommended in pregnancy for women with a short cervix or previous preterm birth to reduce preterm delivery. (NICE NG25; RCOG)

lactation: Natural progesterone is compatible with breastfeeding and does not adversely affect milk supply. (LactMed; ABM Clinical Protocol #13)
warnings: Vaginal use bioavailability variable; oral micronised has hepatic first-pass.
adverseEffects: Breast tenderness, mood change, drowsiness with oral micronised, mild fluid retention
monitoring: Symptom response; bleeding patterns in HRT

indications.text: Reversal of heparin-induced anticoagulation (intra-operative and overdose).

mechanism: Strongly basic peptide neutralising heparin (forms inactive ionic complex).

adult.regimen: 1 mg neutralises ~100 units heparin given in last hour; max 50 mg per dose; over 10 minutes.

pregnancy.notes: Single emergency doses to reverse heparin are used in pregnancy when bleeding risk outweighs the small risk of maternal hypotension and pulmonary vasoconstriction. (BNF; Briggs et al., 11th ed.)

lactation: Single intraoperative or emergency dose only; rapidly cleared and orally inactive in the infant — compatible. (LactMed)
warnings: Severe hypotension and anaphylaxis can occur — give slow IV; calculate dose based on time since heparin.
adverseEffects: Hypotension, bradycardia, anaphylaxis, paradoxical bleeding at high doses
monitoring: BP, HR, aPTT

indications.text: Neovascular AMD, diabetic macular oedema, retinal vein occlusion (intravitreal).

mechanism: Monoclonal antibody fragment neutralising VEGF-A → reduced neovascularisation and oedema.

adult.regimen: 0.5 mg intravitreal monthly until vision stable then PRN per local protocol.

pregnancy.notes: Intravitreal anti-VEGF Fab; systemic exposure is very low but a class effect on placentation is possible. Use only if benefit outweighs risk. (BNF; manufacturer SmPC)

lactation: Very low systemic absorption from intravitreal injection and large protein not orally bioavailable; considered probably compatible. (LactMed)
contraindications: Active or suspected ocular or periocular infection
warnings: Endophthalmitis is the most serious complication of intravitreal injection — sterile technique; monitor for visual loss / eye pain.
adverseEffects: Conjunctival haemorrhage, eye pain, increased IOP, endophthalmitis (rare), retinal detachment
monitoring: IOP measurement post-injection; visual acuity reviews

indications.text: Historically: peptic ulcer, GORD. Largely replaced by famotidine and PPIs.

mechanism: Selective competitive H2-receptor antagonism reducing gastric acid secretion. Recalled in 2020 over NDMA contamination.

adult.regimen: 150 mg twice daily or 300 mg at night.

pregnancy.notes: Withdrawn from many markets in 2020 owing to NDMA contamination. Where still available, no consistent teratogenic signal at therapeutic doses; H2 blockers were historically considered compatible in pregnancy. (BNF; MHRA 2020)

lactation: Excreted in milk but not associated with adverse infant effects; alternatives (famotidine) are now preferred. (LactMed)
warnings: Withdrawn 2020 due to NDMA contamination — not currently marketed; record retained for cross-reference.
adverseEffects: Headache, dizziness, hepatic enzyme elevation, rare blood dyscrasia
monitoring: None routinely

indications.text: Antenatal and postnatal prophylaxis of RhD-negative mothers.

mechanism: Passive anti-D antibody clearing fetal RhD-positive cells before maternal alloimmunisation occurs.

adult.regimen: 1500 IU at 28 weeks (or 500 IU at 28 and 34 weeks).
500 IU within 72 h of delivery (Kleihauer-guided additional dose if FMH > 4 mL).

pregnancy.notes: Anti-D immunoglobulin is recommended for routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 weeks (and after sensitising events) in non-sensitised RhD-negative women, and within 72 hours of delivery of a RhD-positive infant. (NICE TA156; RCOG)

lactation: Compatible with breastfeeding; immunoglobulins do not pose risk to the infant via milk. (LactMed; NICE)
warnings: Use IM unless severe coagulopathy; do not delay routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 weeks.
adverseEffects: Injection-site soreness, mild fever, rare hypersensitivity
monitoring: Maternal anti-D antibody status if circumstances change

indications.text: Prevention of RSV lower respiratory disease (adults ≥60, pregnant 24–36 weeks, infants per nirsevimab eligibility).

mechanism: Adult RSV vaccine: prefusion-F protein subunit; nirsevimab passive antibody for infants.

adult.regimen: Single 0.5 mL IM (e.g. RSVpreF) in adults ≥ 60 years or pregnant 24–36 weeks per local schedule.

pregnancy.notes: Maternal bivalent RSVpreF vaccine (Abrysvo) is recommended in pregnancy between 32+0 and 36+6 weeks to protect the infant from severe RSV disease. Nirsevimab is given to the infant, not the mother. (CDC ACIP; JCVI 2024)

lactation: Maternal RSV vaccine and infant nirsevimab are compatible with breastfeeding. (CDC ACIP)
warnings: Adult vaccine: use in ≥ 60 years per local guidance; maternal vaccination 24–36 weeks gestation provides infant passive immunity.
adverseEffects: Local reactions, headache, fatigue, mild fever
monitoring: 15-min observation post-injection

references.label: BNF — RSV vaccine / monoclonal antibody monograph

mechanism: Colonic sennoside metabolites stimulate myenteric plexus.

adult.regimen: 7.5–15 mg at bedtime, increase to 30 mg if needed; bowel preparation higher dose per protocol.

pregnancy.notes: Stimulant laxative considered acceptable in pregnancy when bulk-forming and osmotic laxatives are insufficient; widely used. (BNF; Briggs et al., 11th ed.)

lactation: Minimal active metabolites in milk; compatible with breastfeeding and not associated with infant diarrhoea at therapeutic maternal doses. (LactMed)
warnings: Avoid prolonged use (> 1 week) — risk of cathartic colon. Onset 6–12 h.
adverseEffects: Abdominal cramps, brown urine discolouration, electrolyte disturbance with chronic abuse
monitoring: None routinely

indications.text: Umbrella record for cross-reference resolution; see specific SSRI for prescribing.

mechanism: Class-level entry. See individual records (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram, fluvoxamine).

adult.regimen: See specific SSRI record (fluoxetine, sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, paroxetine, fluvoxamine).

pregnancy.notes: Class entry: SSRIs are generally continued in pregnancy when clinically indicated. Paroxetine carries an FDA Category D warning for congenital cardiac defects; sertraline is the most commonly preferred SSRI in pregnancy and lactation. Third-trimester exposure may cause neonatal adaptation syndrome and rare persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. (BNF; NICE CG192; FDA labels)

lactation: Class entry: sertraline and paroxetine have the lowest relative infant doses and are the SSRIs of choice during breastfeeding; fluoxetine has a longer half-life and higher milk levels. Monitor the infant for irritability, sleep, and feeding. (LactMed; NICE CG192)
warnings: Class effects: GI upset, sexual dysfunction, hyponatraemia (especially elderly), increased bleeding risk, discontinuation syndrome.
adverseEffects: Class effects above; serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs
monitoring: Mood and suicidality especially first weeks; sodium in elderly

mechanism: Binds D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of cell-wall precursors → inhibits Gram-positive cell-wall synthesis.

adult.regimen: Loading 400 mg every 12 h for 3 doses, then 400 mg daily; adjust by trough levels and renal function.

pregnancy.notes: Limited human data; manufacturer advises avoid unless potential benefit outweighs risk. Has been used for serious Gram-positive infection in pregnancy. (BNF; manufacturer SmPC)

lactation: No published data on transfer into human milk; poor oral bioavailability suggests minimal infant exposure. Use with monitoring. (LactMed)
warnings: Nephrotoxic in combination with other nephrotoxins.
Vancomycin cross-reactivity is partial — use cautiously after vancomycin reactions.
Adjust dose by renal function.
adverseEffects: Rash, pruritus
Fever, anaphylaxis (rare)
Nephrotoxicity (less than vancomycin)
Thrombocytopenia, eosinophilia
Ototoxicity (rare)
monitoring: Trough level ≥ 15 mg/L for serious infections
Renal function and FBC during prolonged therapy

indications.text: See specific tenofovir record for prescribing; this slug exists for cross-reference resolution.

mechanism: Phosphorylated to tenofovir diphosphate; chain terminator of HIV/HBV reverse transcriptase. See tenofovir-disoproxil-fumarate (TDF) and tenofovir-alafenamide (TAF).

adult.regimen: TDF 245 mg once daily / TAF 25 mg once daily per indication.

pregnancy.notes: Class umbrella entry: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is the preferred prodrug in pregnancy for HIV and chronic HBV with extensive safety data; tenofovir alafenamide data are growing and now supported by WHO 2023. (WHO HIV; DHHS perinatal)

lactation: Class umbrella entry: low milk transfer and very low oral bioavailability — WHO recommends continuation of effective maternal ART during breastfeeding. (WHO; LactMed)
warnings: Class warnings: nephrotoxicity, bone-mineral-density loss; HBV flare on stopping in coinfection. See specific TDF / TAF record for prescribing.
adverseEffects: Nephrotoxicity, decreased BMD, GI upset, asthenia
monitoring: eGFR, phosphate, urine glucose/protein; bone-mineral density in long-term

indications.text: Confirmed hypogonadism (per endocrinology); transgender hormone therapy.

mechanism: Selective androgen-receptor agonist on muscle, bone and secondary sexual tissues.

adult.regimen: Testosterone undecanoate 1 g IM every 10–14 weeks.
Testosterone gel 40–60 mg/day applied to clean dry skin.

pregnancy: Contraindicated in pregnancy; counsel female partners.
lactation: Suppresses lactation; not indicated in lactating women. (BNF; LactMed)
warnings: Polycythaemia — check haematocrit; pause if > 54%.
Increased thrombotic risk in older men with cardiovascular disease.
Avoid skin-to-skin contact with women/children after gel application.
adverseEffects: Acne, increased aggressiveness, polycythaemia, sleep apnoea worsening, PSA rise
monitoring: Haematocrit, lipids, PSA, prostate examination

indications.text: Routine immunisation and post-injury booster; tetanus prophylaxis.

mechanism: Inactivated Clostridium tetani toxoid inducing protective antitoxin antibodies.

adult.regimen: 0.5 mL IM; primary series + boosters per national schedule; post-injury booster if last dose > 10 years or unclean wound > 5 years.

pregnancy.notes: Tetanus toxoid (and Tdap) is recommended in pregnancy — WHO Maternal and Neonatal Tetanus Elimination programme; Tdap recommended each pregnancy at 16–32 weeks in many national schedules. (WHO; CDC ACIP; UK Green Book)

lactation: Inactivated toxoid — compatible with breastfeeding. (CDC ACIP; UK Green Book)
contraindications: Anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component
warnings: Live vaccines: avoid in immunosuppression and pregnancy. Counsel about expected mild fever/local reactions.
adverseEffects: Injection-site soreness, redness; low-grade fever; rare anaphylaxis
monitoring: 15-min observation post-injection where anaphylaxis kit not immediately available

indications.text: Multiple myeloma (combination); leprosy ENL reactions. ABSOLUTELY teratogenic — pregnancy prevention programme mandatory.

mechanism: Cereblon-binding immunomodulation with anti-angiogenic, anti-TNF and direct cytotoxic effects.

adult.regimen: 100–200 mg at bedtime cycled per regimen.
100–300 mg at bedtime; taper to lowest effective.

pregnancy.notes: Severely teratogenic (phocomelia, cardiac and other defects) — absolutely contraindicated. Mandatory pregnancy prevention programme with two methods of contraception required for women of child-bearing potential. (BNF; MHRA; Pregnancy Prevention Programme)

lactation: No human data; manufacturer advises avoid because of teratogenic potential and theoretical infant exposure. (BNF; LactMed)
contraindications: Inability to comply with pregnancy prevention programme
warnings: Mandatory pregnancy prevention programme (CRPP) with pregnancy testing for women of childbearing potential.
Risk of VTE — consider antithrombotic prophylaxis.
Peripheral neuropathy — examine before each prescription.
adverseEffects: Severe teratogenicity, VTE, peripheral neuropathy, drowsiness, constipation, bradycardia, rash
monitoring: Pregnancy testing per CRPP; clinical neuropathy assessment; FBC

indications.text: Severe asthma, COPD (when other inhaled therapies inadequate).

mechanism: Non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibition and adenosine-receptor antagonism; narrow therapeutic index.

adult.regimen: Modified-release 200–400 mg twice daily; individualise by level.

pregnancy.notes: Generally considered compatible when needed for asthma or COPD control; monitor levels — clearance changes in the third trimester. Neonates exposed near term may show irritability and tachycardia. (BNF; Briggs et al., 11th ed.)

lactation: Excreted in milk; usually compatible at therapeutic maternal doses but monitor the infant for irritability and feeding. (LactMed; BNF)
warnings: Narrow therapeutic index (10–20 mg/L) — monitor serum levels.
Many interactions: ciprofloxacin, macrolides, fluvoxamine raise levels; rifampicin, smoking, phenytoin lower.
Reduce dose in heart failure, hepatic disease, the elderly and febrile illness.
adverseEffects: GI upset, headache, insomnia
Palpitations, tachyarrhythmia
Seizures (toxic levels)
Hypokalaemia in overdose
monitoring: Serum theophylline 4–6 h after oral dose at steady state; K⁺ in acute exacerbation

mechanism: Closes pancreatic beta-cell K-ATP channels → insulin secretion. CYP2C9 metabolism (PGx target).

adult.regimen: 0.5–2 g/day in divided doses; largely superseded.

pregnancy.notes: Limited modern data; switch to insulin in pregnancy. Sulphonylureas can cause prolonged neonatal hypoglycaemia if used near term. (BNF; NICE NG3)

lactation: Small amounts in milk; risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia — manufacturer advises avoid. (BNF; LactMed)
warnings: CYP2C9 substrate — variable response by genotype.
adverseEffects: Hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, rash
monitoring: HbA1c, capillary glucose

indications.text: Mild eczema, dermatitis, insect bites (face-safe, short-course).

mechanism: Glucocorticoid receptor agonist with anti-inflammatory effect at the application site.

adult.regimen: 0.5% or 1% cream/ointment applied thinly once or twice daily for up to 7 days.

pregnancy.notes: Topical hydrocortisone (mild potency) is considered compatible across pregnancy; use the smallest effective amount for the shortest duration and avoid extensive or occlusive use. (BNF; NICE)

lactation: Compatible with breastfeeding. If applied to the nipple, wipe off immediately before feeding. (LactMed; BNF)
contraindications: Untreated bacterial, viral or fungal skin infection
warnings: Avoid prolonged use on face and flexures; thinning of skin with prolonged use.
adverseEffects: Skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis with prolonged use
monitoring: Skin response; switch to potent steroid if no response after 2 weeks

indications.text: VTE treatment in renal failure, ACS, cardiopulmonary bypass, dialysis circuit.

mechanism: Antithrombin-mediated inactivation of thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa; aPTT-monitored.

adult.regimen: 80 units/kg IV bolus then 18 units/kg/h, adjust to aPTT 1.5–2.5× control.
5000 units every 8–12 h.

pregnancy.notes: Does not cross the placenta; anticoagulant of choice for VTE in pregnancy where rapid reversibility or renal impairment limits LMWH use. (BNF; RCOG Green-top 37a/37b)

lactation: Not excreted in significant amounts in milk and poorly absorbed orally; compatible with breastfeeding. (LactMed)
contraindications: History of HIT (unless not reactive on assay)
warnings: Monitor aPTT or anti-Xa during therapeutic infusion.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — type II onset day 4–14; stop heparin if platelets fall by ≥ 50%.
Risk of epidural haematoma with neuraxial anaesthesia within hours of dose.
adverseEffects: Bleeding, thrombocytopenia (HIT), hyperkalaemia, osteoporosis with long-term use, skin necrosis
monitoring: aPTT 6 h after starting infusion and after dose changes; platelet count baseline and twice-weekly

indications.text: Routine paediatric immunisation (per local schedule); susceptible healthcare workers.

mechanism: Live attenuated Oka-strain varicella virus inducing humoral and cellular immunity.

adult.regimen: Two doses 4–8 weeks apart.

pregnancy.notes: Live attenuated vaccine — contraindicated in pregnancy; avoid pregnancy for 1 month after vaccination. (CDC ACIP; UK Green Book)

lactation: Compatible with breastfeeding — vaccine virus has not been transmitted via milk. (CDC ACIP; LactMed)
warnings: Avoid salicylate use for 6 weeks post-vaccination (Reye syndrome risk).
Avoid conception within 1 month of vaccination.
adverseEffects: Injection-site reaction, mild varicelliform rash 1–4 weeks later, fever
monitoring: Pregnancy status before administration in women of childbearing age

indications.text: Pernicious anaemia, dietary B12 deficiency, B12-deficient neuropathy.

mechanism: Cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase.

adult.regimen: Hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM three times weekly for 2 weeks, then 1 mg every 2–3 months.
1 mg IM on alternate days until improvement, then 1 mg every 2 months.

pregnancy.notes: B12 replacement is recommended in pregnancy where deficiency is identified; physiological requirements increase. (BNF; WHO)

lactation: Maternal B12 is excreted in milk and supports normal infant intake; replacement is compatible with breastfeeding. (LactMed)
warnings: Hydroxocobalamin preferred over cyanocobalamin in UK schedules; do not give as IV bolus.
adverseEffects: Itching, rash, headache, hypokalaemia on starting treatment of megaloblastic anaemia (monitor potassium)
monitoring: FBC and reticulocyte response; potassium during initial treatment of megaloblastic anaemia

indications.text: Vitamin D deficiency, osteoporosis adjunct, prevention of rickets/osteomalacia.

mechanism: Activates vitamin D receptor → calcium and phosphate homeostasis, bone mineralisation.

adult.regimen: Colecalciferol 50 000 IU once weekly for 6 weeks, then 800–2000 IU/day maintenance.

pregnancy.notes: Routine supplementation (10 micrograms / 400 IU daily) is recommended for all pregnant women in many national guidelines. Higher doses for deficiency. (NICE PH56; RCOG Scientific Impact Paper 43)

lactation: Maternal supplementation is recommended; breastfed infants should receive separate vitamin D supplementation per local schedule. (NICE; AAP)
warnings: Risk of hypercalcaemia with high doses; ensure renal function adequate.
adverseEffects: Hypercalcaemia, nephrocalcinosis with chronic high doses, nausea
monitoring: Serum 25(OH)D, calcium, phosphate, ALP at baseline; calcium during high-dose loading

indications.text: Post-exposure prophylaxis in susceptible high-risk contacts (pregnant, immunocompromised, neonates).

mechanism: Passive anti-VZV antibody for post-exposure prophylaxis.

adult.regimen: 1000 mg in non-pregnant; 1000 mg + monitoring in pregnancy (or aciclovir prophylaxis per local guideline).

pregnancy.notes: Passive immunoglobulin; recommended post-exposure prophylaxis for non-immune pregnant women exposed to varicella (where seronegative). (RCOG Green-top 13; UK Green Book)

lactation: Immunoglobulin preparations are compatible with breastfeeding. (LactMed)
warnings: Administer within 10 days (preferably 4) of exposure; benefit beyond 10 days unclear.
adverseEffects: Injection-site reactions, fever, anaphylaxis (rare)
monitoring: Clinical follow-up for VZV development

indications.text: WHO IMCI adjunct in childhood acute diarrhoea; zinc deficiency.

mechanism: Mineral cofactor for innate immunity and gut epithelial integrity; WHO IMCI adjunct in acute diarrhoea.

adult.regimen: Children: 10 mg/day (< 6 months) or 20 mg/day (≥ 6 months) for 10–14 days.
15–30 mg/day elemental zinc.

pregnancy.notes: Replacement at RDA is recommended where dietary intake is inadequate; avoid high-dose supplementation (>40 mg elemental/day) outside a supervised indication. (BNF; WHO)

lactation: Physiological supplementation compatible with breastfeeding; avoid high-dose chronic use which can impair maternal copper status. (LactMed)
warnings: High doses can cause copper deficiency and reduce immune function.
adverseEffects: Nausea, abdominal pain, metallic taste; copper deficiency with chronic high doses
monitoring: Copper status in prolonged supplementation

mechanism: Selective alpha-1 subunit GABA-A receptor agonism; short-acting.

adult.regimen: 5–10 mg at bedtime; halve in elderly.

pregnancy.notes: No consistent teratogenic signal; third-trimester use may cause neonatal sedation, hypotonia, and withdrawal. Use occasional lowest effective dose. (BNF; Briggs et al., 11th ed.)

lactation: Low milk levels (~0.02% of maternal weight-adjusted dose); occasional use considered compatible with breastfeeding. (LactMed)
warnings: Risk of dependence — limit to ≤ 4 weeks.
Next-day driving impairment — caution with morning activities.
Halve dose in elderly.
adverseEffects: Drowsiness, dizziness, headache, anterograde amnesia, complex sleep behaviour (rare)
monitoring: Re-evaluate need at each prescription

mechanism: Sodium- and T-type calcium-channel blockade, weak carbonic anhydrase inhibition.

adult.regimen: 50 mg/day; titrate by 50 mg every 2 weeks to 300–500 mg/day in two divided doses.

pregnancy.notes: Associated with low birth weight and an increased risk of major congenital malformations; if continued, use lowest effective dose with high-dose folic acid (5 mg/day). (BNF; MHRA 2021)

lactation: Excreted in milk in significant amounts with infant plasma levels approaching maternal; avoid where alternatives exist, or monitor the infant closely for sedation and feeding. (LactMed)
warnings: Risk of metabolic acidosis and renal stones (carbonic anhydrase inhibition).
Weight loss possible; avoid in patients with anorexia/eating disorder.
Heat-stroke risk in children — avoid in hot weather.
adverseEffects: Somnolence, dizziness, GI upset, weight loss, paraesthesia, oligohidrosis, renal stones
monitoring: Renal stones screening; serum bicarbonate periodically

mechanism: GABA-A receptor positive modulator (cyclopyrrolone class).

adult.regimen: 7.5 mg at bedtime; elderly 3.75 mg.

pregnancy.notes: Limited data; third-trimester use may cause neonatal sedation, hypotonia, and withdrawal. Use occasional lowest effective dose. (BNF; Briggs et al., 11th ed.)

lactation: Excreted in milk in low amounts; occasional use considered probably compatible — avoid prolonged use and monitor the infant for sedation. (LactMed)
warnings: Bitter or metallic taste common; dependence risk — ≤ 4 weeks; elderly half-dose.
adverseEffects: Drowsiness, taste disturbance, dry mouth, dizziness, amnesia
monitoring: Re-evaluate at each prescription
